title: Trust, Worries and Self Improvement
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart's main teaching is that our worries can be overwhelming, but by learning to observe them without getting caught up in their demands, we can find freedom from mental clutter. Through the example of a "worry box" filled with concerns, Kanho illustrates how our minds can be easily distracted and prioritized, but also shows how Zen practice allows us to take out these worries one by one, allowing for greater awareness and freedom. By letting go of conditioning and expectations, we can discover that true happiness and fulfillment come from within, rather than from external sources or achievements.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed penetrating and perfect dharma, is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Good morning, everyone.
It's wonderful to see you.
I'm just going to click through so I can actually see everybody.
It still feels strange to be on screen in our dharma relations.
So thank you for being here today, and thank you very much for the sitting together.
It is a wonderful support for me, even though our togetherness is only electronic and not live.
But that's all right.
Sitting together is the best, no matter what shape it takes.
I'm really excited that in about a month, on November 6, we will have the opportunity to sit together in person.
This is our first in-person Red Cedar event in a long, long time.
The last one was March 2020.
And that's really, really sweet.
It gets even better.
The retreat will end with the lay entrustment ceremony for Haikaku Talus Latona, and I'm so happy about that.
I'm looking forward to what Talus is going to contribute as a lay entrusted member.
But I am also a little bit sad, because it means that Talus is done sewing his rakusu, and we will lose him in our Sunday evening Zen sewing circle.
So, a few details about the retreat.
It will happen in the Shambhala Center on Meridian in Bellingham.
You may join us in person or you can zoom in.
It is a first for us: it's going to be the first live online hybrid event that Red Cedar is sponsoring.
Please be aware that if you want to come in person, you need to be fully vaccinated.
If you'd like more information, please check out our website.
You need to register for this event, because only a limited number of participants will be allowed in the room due to continuing COVID precautions.
Talking about practicing together, I'm sure you've all heard about the fundraising campaign that we are engaged in right now.
Maybe you've participated in meetings with our consultants, or you have received calls as part of the fundraising effort.
The process around all this is quite fascinating in itself.
So much goes on in my mind when I listen to the different proposals.
It's very interesting what is valued, what is high in priorities and what's low in priorities.
And then, of course, there is the money question.
So I encourage you to give early and to give often.
A warm thank you to all of you who have donated or pledged or are thinking about it.
Because let's face it, not everybody is in a position to give money to this effort, and that's quite all right.
It's interesting: I put a little "please donate" thing on Facebook and I got $500 out of it that will go into that kitty.
I'm pretty excited about that too.
Sometimes I'm intimidated by our wish list, especially when considering real estate prices in Bellingham.
I really trust that something is going to come out of this process and that it will be enough.
I have a lot of trust in our Sangha, and I'm especially grateful to all the Sangha members who have invested their time and energy and knowledge to further this process.
It will be nice to practice again as a community in one space, to actually have a live doanryo.
That said, many thanks to all the hands that make these online events possible.
Thank you.
Bob Penny has been here as our ino.
Desiree has also been active in the doanryo, but she's on the road today.

Another thing that brings me quite a bit of joy is that we're planning to continue hybrid practice, even once the COVID scare is over, to reach out to people who either cannot travel or who live too far away to come to our events.
Sometimes I worry about stuff: whether we will find what we were looking for, and whether owning a Zendo will take too much energy away from our main purpose, which is Zen practice.
Worrying is a very old habit with me, and a pretty useless one too.
I understand from doing Dokusan with various people that I'm not the only one bitten by the worry bug.
So my talk today will be relatively brief, because I would like to have some extra time for conversation about two topics.
Topic number one, as you may have guessed, is worrying thoughts.
The other topic is self-improvement.
More about that later.
I did want to bring up worries.
I have quite a few of them.
Quite often, when the subject of worries comes up, I remember a short story by Ed McManus.
He's a kind of funny outdoor writer.
The name of the story is "The Worry Box."
I won't read you the whole thing, just my favorite part.
So this is now Ed McManus speaking, or writing.
*I have this theory that people possess a certain capacity for worry, no more, no less.
It's as though a person has a little psychic box that he feels compelled to keep filled with worries.
When one worry disappears from the box, he immediately replaces it with another worry.
So the box is always full.
He's never short of worries.
If a new crop of worries comes in, the person sorts through the box for lesser worries and kicks them out until he has enough room for new worries.
The lesser worries just lie around on the floor until there is room in the box for them again, and then they are put back in.*
Now, a short comment: Bun is his wife.
*Where Bun really excels in worry production for me is on camping trips.
It is popularly thought that camping provides a wonderful way to escape from the stresses of modern life.
I myself think this too.
I can always tell it's time to head for the mountains when I start getting stress cramps in my eyelids.
They're quite painful and caused me to go about for days with a startled, somewhat horrified expression.
People coming toward me on the sidewalk look at me, then jerk their heads around to see what's sneaking up behind them.
It's an embarrassment, not to mention a major social liability.
Once I'm back in the mountain store and Bun and I set up our tent and roll out our sleeping bags, the stress cramps vanish from my eyelids.
Soon I'm drifting into a deep and peaceful slumber, the fragrances of leaf mold and cedar boughs caressing my nostrils.
It's nice.*
*"Wasn't you?"
Bun asks.*
*"Nope.
Probably just leaf mold."*
*"No, I don't mean that.
I mean that snuffling.
Did you just snuffle?"*
*"I don't think so," I reply, trying to recall the characteristics of a snuffle.
"Oh well, go to sleep.
It was probably just my imagination."
Yeah, but maybe not, I think.
Maybe something outside the tent snuffled.
A bird wouldn't snuffle.
Squirrels and chipmunks are too small to snuffle.
Something would have to be pretty big to snuffle.
A deer would make a similar sound, but not a true snuffle.
Actually, the only animal I've ever heard do a true snuffle is a bear.*
*"For heaven's sake, what's wrong now?"
Bun asks.*
*"I have lid cramps.*"
So that's Ed McManus on a worry box.
Here's an interesting aspect of my own worry theory.
*Up to the point where Bun mentions the snuffle, my worry box is neatly layered with worries about the children, work, money, illness, poverty, pestilence, environment, war, a checkbook, famine, etc.
Each patiently awaiting its turn for my attention.
But the instant the snuffle is mentioned and its source identified as bear, all those other worries are plastered right out of the box by the sudden inflation of the snuffle worry.
War, poverty, pestilence, why they couldn't even be shoehorned back into my worry box.
It's packed so tight with snuffle.*
End of McManus.
So this is the story about the worry box, and I have a worry box too.
In fact, most people I know have indicated one way or the other that they too have a worry box.
Sometimes we find that we have taken the old worry box to the cushion with us.

The worry box may tell us that if we were smarter, younger, stronger, more in control (that's a big one), more accomplished; if we studied more, if we made more money, if we had the right job and that raise; if we had met the fairy tale prince or princess; if we had kids, or the right kids, then, yes, finally, we would be happy.
And in the meantime, we worry about all those things.

Speaking for myself, there was a lot of conditioning in my early life around all these subjects: about what I was supposed to be like, what I was supposed to look like, how I was supposed to work, how I was supposed to study.
When I failed to meet expectations, the expectations of my parents or my teachers, I felt at fault.
I felt that I was blameworthy and that I was in sore need of being fixed, improved.
You can probably fill in your own story here.
The sad thing is that these expectations went on and on and on.
They changed over time, of course, from high school grades to prospective husbands and the prospective number of kids.
Don't get me wrong.
I do not mean to criticize my parents.
They did what they did without ill will, and my best was always on their mind.
They wanted me to grow up the very best way.
And they wanted me, as I realized later, to live the life they had wanted for themselves.
Culturally and in my family, I did not see a lot of leeway, alternatives or options.
Growing up, we accept so much that is presented to us and imposed on us.
Well, to cut a long story short, I ran.
The width of two continents and one ocean is a pretty long way.
But I was stuck with this conditioned mind.
Now in retrospect, I think it's sad that I accepted the conditioning for as long as I did.
In summary, let me say that all this has left me with a well-built, good-sized industrial worry box.
And maybe it's also good that I take this worry box to the cushion with me.
In fact, I do need to take the worry box with me to the cushion, because that is the only place that I've found where I can deconstruct it.
So I take the worry box with me.
I know how to sit until the time is right.
I know how to gently and softly open the box.
I now have practice in taking out a worry, some conditioning, and investigating it for what it is.
Not all the things in the worry box need to be thrown out.
Some of them are valuable pointers.
Practice has created a space, a gap, where I have freedom to choose what to do with this worry.
I don't need to follow old programming or simply do the opposite, which is the same thing with a rebellious undertone.
Some of the worries and conditioning aspects need to be taken out more than once.
Some need much attention over a very long time.
One thing about conditioning that I've found is that it is so grounded in duality and comparison and competition.
Here's a poem by Leonard Cohen, who was a Zen monk for some time.
It's titled "Roshi."
I never really understood what he said.
But every now and then, I find myself barking with the dog or bending with the irises or helping out in other little ways.
So sometimes I kick out some worries and put in a poem instead, to remind me what to do with what's left in the box.
I love this little poem, and I don't really understand it.
Every now and then, though, I do find myself mumbling with my chickens and moving with the wind and hiking up a mountain.
Zen practice allows us to simply be, not do, not achieve, just be human.
We can observe conditioned mind without being caught up in its demands and its shoulds and its must-do's.
The Buddha said many times that just as the great ocean has but one taste, the taste of salt, so do all the true teachings of the Dharma contain the taste of freedom.
Taking the step from blindly following conditioning to observing conditioning can be difficult, because oftentimes we don't even realize that the conditioning exists.
It's so ingrained, it's so part of us, that it takes time and love to do it.
In this process, it is important to avoid a misunderstanding: Zen is not a self-improvement project.
It feels paradoxical.
Yes, Zen practice has been very beneficial for me.
But Zen practice for the purpose of self-improvement just isn't it.
Self-improvement is such an ego thing, such an ego activity.
It usually focuses on the acquisition of goals, achievements and experiences.
It's quite wonderful to have a meditation experience, and sometimes they happen, often to some, and for others it's super rare.

That self-improvement drive might have us end up in a mindfulness course or a zendo to achieve something, while utterly ignoring the quality of big mind, the quality of consciousness that can come out of this experience.
If we are busy with self-improvement, we are guaranteed to miss those sweet and tender moments.
So self-improvement, which focuses on gaining, on acquisition, is not going to help us on the cushion.
Our purpose, if I can call it that, which still misses the boat, is not success or improving a position.
It's simply understanding, or coming closer to understanding, one's true Buddha nature, one's true self-nature.
Let's not get caught in the false belief that happiness is something that can be attained outside of us, but rather realize that it is within, right here and right now.
Now, we'd like to end today's talk with a poem by Katagiri Roshi.
I've quoted this poem before, so if you've heard it before, it's one of my favorites, and I will probably continue to read it.
*Being told that it is impossible, one believes in despair.
Is that so?
Being told that it is possible, one believes in excitement.
That's right.
But whichever is chosen, it does not fit one's heart neatly.
Being asked, what is unfitting?
I don't know what it is, but my heart knows somehow.
I feel irresistible desire to know what a mystery human is.
As to this mystery, clarifying, knowing how to live, knowing how to talk with people, demonstrating and teaching.
This is the Buddha.
When I look into human eyes, I feel it's really impossible to become Buddha.
But this I, regarding what the Buddha does, vows to practice, to aspire, to be resolute, and tells myself, yes, I will.
Let's practice right here now and achieve continuity, endlessly, forever.
This is living in vow.
Herein is one's peaceful life found.*
*May our intention equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
